claims.text: Introducing surface oxygen vacancies enhances ethanol-oxidation activity.
Introducing surface oxygen vacancies improves selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Introducing surface oxygen vacancies improves catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
The catalytic effect of the proposed modification is mediated by changes in local electronic structure.
Surface oxygen vacancies shift the d-band center of the catalyst.
Surface oxygen vacancies increase the density of catalytically active sites.
The as-synthesized catalyst has a native surface oxidation state with a minimal oxygen-vacancy concentration.
A mild reduction or plasma treatment can systematically induce a measurable surface oxygen-vacancy concentration in the catalyst.
Ethanol oxidation on the relevant multimetallic catalyst can proceed through a 12-electron process.
The relevant ethanol-oxidation process involves 12-proton transfer.
Induced oxygen vacancies alter the catalyst surface oxidation state and local atomic configuration.
A vacancy-induced d-band-center change improves adsorption and desorption kinetics of ethanol and its intermediates.
Changes in electronic properties can regulate adsorbate binding energies on platinum-containing high-entropy-alloy catalysts.
Oxygen vacancies enhance coupled electron-proton transfer efficiency during ethanol oxidation.
Oxygen vacancies mitigate catalyst-deactivation pathways.
Vacancy-treated catalysts will show higher oxidation current density than untreated catalysts.
Vacancy-treated catalysts will favor complete-oxidation products over partial-oxidation products.
Vacancy-treated catalysts will retain activity better during prolonged cycling than untreated catalysts.
The proposed vacancy mechanism may cease to influence performance outside the targeted electrochemical potential window or in non-electrochemical catalysis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in any of current density, complete-oxidation selectivity, or durability would falsify the hypothesis.
